question: Will Venezuela be elected to the IAEA Board of Governors at the 70th General Conference?

calls.reasoning: Venezuela was elected at GC68 (Sept 2024) for 2024-2026, so its seat is one of the 11 expiring at GC70. The IAEA Statute (Art. VI, as reflected in GC records and the GC Rules of Procedure) makes retiring elected members ineligible for re-election for the immediately following term — GC(55)/OR.8 records outgoing African members Cameroon and Kenya as 'ineligible under Article VI.A.2 of the Statute for re-election', and ballots naming ineligible members are invalid. Independent empirical check: comparing elected cohorts two years apart (GC66-2022 vs GC68-2024; GC67-2023 vs GC69-2025) yields 0 of 33 immediate re-elections, with Saudi Arabia (elected 2022, again 2025) and Colombia (2021, again 2024) showing the one-session gap the rule implies. The question's framing appears to assume a routine re-election contest, but the outcome looks rule-determined rather than politically contested; Venezuela's strained diplomatic standing only reinforces the direction. No human market prices this (Kalshi and Polymarket carry Venezuela political markets, none on IAEA governance); the GC70 candidate memorandum was not yet published as of 2026-09-07. Residual probability covers the chance my reading of the eligibility bar is wrong (I could not open the primary Statute text — iaea.org returned 402/403 to direct fetches) or that Venezuela somehow appears in the elected slate.

VI.A.2(a), enforced by GC Rules of Procedure Rule 85, makes a retiring elected member ineligible for immediate re-election in the same category — ballots cast for such a state are invalid (cf. GC(55)/OR.8, where outgoing Cameroon and Kenya were recorded as ineligible). Latin America & Caribbean holds only Art. VI.A.2(a) elective seats and has no access to the rotating (b)/(c) seats, so there is no category-switch workaround of the kind that likely let the Republic of Korea appear in both the 2021 and 2023 cohorts. Empirically, consecutive IAEA elected cohorts 2022->2024 and 2023->2025 show zero overlap, and no GRULAC state has been re-elected consecutively in 2021-2025. The three GRULAC seats up at GC70 are Argentina, Colombia and Venezuela's — all three incumbents are barred, so the seats go to other GRULAC states (Ecuador/Paraguay are eligible again, plus Cuba, Mexico, Bolivia, Uruguay, Costa Rica, etc.). US-Venezuela tensions and Venezuela's active IAEA technical cooperation are both largely irrelevant given the statutory bar. No prediction market prices this. calls.reconciliation: All three runs reached 0.02-0.03 by the same mechanism, so the reconciliation question was whether the convergence is earned or a shared error. Disputed: (a) where the eligibility bar lives in the Statute — Run 1 said Art. VI.A.2, Run 2 Art. VI.A.2(a) enforced via GC Rules of Procedure Rule 85, Run 3 Art. VI.B. Unsettled on this run (no web access; all three fetchers were blocked by iaea.org HTTP 402/403), and I let it carry its uncertainty rather than picking a citation by fiat. It does not change the estimate, because the bar's existence is corroborated by two lines independent of the citation: the verbatim GC(55)/OR.8 record of outgoing Cameroon and Kenya being ruled ineligible for re-election, cited identically by two runs, and the cohort data. (b) The empirical rate: Run 1 reported 0/33, Runs 2 and 3 reported 1/33. Settled for 1/33 — Runs 2 and 3 both list Republic of Korea in the 2021 and 2023 cohorts and Run 1's own cohort lists contain the same two Korea entries, so 0/33 is an arithmetic slip in Run 1, not a different reading of the record. This is the conservative direction and I adopted it. Run 2's explanation (Korea switching between an A.2(a) quota seat and a rotating A.2(b) seat open to Asian groups) is the only account offered for the exception; Run 3 flagged it unexplained. I carried Run 2's reading because it is mechanistic and, if right, removes the exception from Venezuela's class entirely — GRULAC has only A.2(a) seats. (c) Whether Venezuela's degraded diplomatic standing matters: judgment, and near-irrelevant either way, since a statutory bar does not care about political standing; it only makes an already-unlikely exception less likely. I did not average the runs. I landed at 0.025, at the low end rather than the middle, because the two corroborating lines (an applied primary-source precedent, and a 1/33 base rate whose single exception has a structural explanation excluding GRULAC) are close to independent, which is stronger than any single run's case. I held above 0.02 rather than going lower because no run could render the primary Statute text and the question's own background frames this as a live contest — leaving a real, if small, chance the bar is narrower than all three runs read it. Market check confirmed: no venue prices IAEA Board composition; the Polymarket/Kalshi Venezuela contracts match neither subject, deadline, nor resolution source, so they are evidence about Venezuelan politics, not an anchor here.
